commit.message: Remove existing biasPhysReg logic from scheduler; produces strangely long live ranges in some cases.

Teach MachineScheduler how to load A,X,Y for calls.

Generally, A needs to be loaded last, preceeded by X and Y, preceeded by
everything else. This is because A is often useful for loading X and Y,
and GPRs are often useful for loading zero page registers and stack. The
inverse is true for return values.

This adds a clause to the scheduler encoding this preference. The
original biasPhysReg() call is also restored; we actually do need to
keep physreg live ranges as short as possible, or the register allocator
chokes on large examples (printf).

Squashed commit of the MOS code generator.

    Make ZP_PTR_1 and ZP_PTR_3 callee-saved-registers (CSRs).

    We need at least one CSR pointer, since that's how LLVM handles
    saving frame pointers around calls. Accordingly, we dedicate ZP_PTR_1
    to this purpose. The minimum number of ZP pointer registers is
    accordingly bumped to 2, since we may need at minimum one for addressing
    and one for a frame pointer.

    We also allocate ZP_PTR_3 as a second CSR. We set the threshold for
    using a CSR quite high, since saving and restoring one is often much
    worse than using the hard stack. Only 2 ZP pointers make sense to be
    CSRs, since we allocate 4 bytes of hard stack per frame, and saving
    them to the soft stack is even more expensive. We also want as many
    regs as possible available for call arguments.

    Don't bias physical registers to their uses.

    The scheduler previously would strongly shorten the live ranges of
    physical registers, even if that increased the register pressure for
    virtual registers. Since our virtual registers classes often *are*
    physical registers, this doesn't make sense on our platform.

    This was the original reason to make 1-element register classes, so it
    may be possible to go through and rewrite instructions to implicitly
    use-def physical registers again. This probably isn't a good idea
    though: LLVM optimization passes (e.g., TwoAddressPass) generally expect
    operations to have a certain RISCy shape, and they'll disable themselves
    if the observed shape differs.

    Lower C structs to non-byval pointers.

    By default, clang lowers C structs to byval pointers, but the
    interpretation of byval is quite target-specific, and it doesn't
    seem to work very well with GlobalISel. Following the example of
    the furthest-along GlobalISel target, AArch64, structs are instead
    lowered to non-byval indirect pointers. This produces the expected
    behavior: argument copies are only made in the caller, and a pointer is
    passed to the copy. This works quite nicely with static stacks, as the
    pointer can be to the caller's static stack; such pointers can be
    generated with only compiler-time arithmetic.

    Allow inline assembly statements to be __attribute__((leaf)).

    This allows the user to guarantee that inline assembly snippets will
    not call back into the translation unit. This is extremely important
    for efficient 6502 code generation, since otherwise any routine
    containing inline assembly (i.e., essentially every OS call) would
    cause the entire call stack to be possibly-recursive, since the syscall
    could technically call main.

    Regularize soft and hard stack access.

    The instruction selector and register allocator now generate generic stk
    pseudoinstructions for register saves and restores and address
    calculations. Once the stack frame layout is finalized, these are
    lowered into more specific pseudoinstructions that reference either the
    hard or soft stack pointer, depending on which stack the slot was
    allocated to.

    Register saves and restores to soft stack slots more than a page above
    the stack pointer are not yet supported, since they'll need virtual base
    pointers to be efficient. This should be done via LLVMs existing virtual
    base pointer generation mechanism (LocalStackSlotAllocation).

    Lower G_LHS 1 to target-specific G_LSHO and G_LSHE instructions.

    G_LSHO and G_LSHE correspondg to ROL and ASL, respectively. They form a
    parallel with G_UADDO and G_UADDE: the "even" (E) versions both produce
    and accept a carry, while the "odd" (O) versions produce a carry but
    implicitly take the carry in to be zero.

    A G_LSHO -> G_LSHE -> G_LSHE ... chain thus corresponds to a ASL, ROL,
    ROL ... chain, shifting multiple bytes left using the carry to
    communicate bites between bytes.

    Only a constant left shift by one is supported. Since the 6502 does not
    have a barrel shifter, shifts by custom amounts will later need to be
    handled by a libcall.

    Allow indexed addressing mode for loads.

    Scans loops to determine when loaded pointers can be built using induction
    variables that provably fit within 8 bits. Rewrites such loops to build
    the pointer zero extending the 8-bit induction variable then GEP-ing the
    base.

    Once such loops make it to the target, legalization identifies
    16-bit G_PTR_ADDs that are sourced from 8-bit G_ZEXT and allows
    them through. Then, such G_PTR_ADDs can be folded with the loads
    to produce an indexed addressing pseudo: LDidx.

    Finally, LDidx is lowered post RA to a real 6502 instruction:
    LDAidx, LDXidx, or LDYidx.
